title: Nvidia Wins Modal as Vera CPU Customer in Push Beyond GPUs
excerpt: The AI cloud startup, valued at $15.75 billion after a $750 million raise, will adopt Nvidia's Vera processor alongside Intel and AMD after tests doubled agent workloads — a design win, not an acquisition.
body:
• Nvidia has won CPU business — not an acquisition — from Modal, the fast-growing AI cloud startup that until now ran its agent-hosting work only on Intel and AMD chips.
  • Modal said early tests showed Nvidia's new Vera processor doubled the amount of work AI agents can complete, prompting it to support Nvidia's chip design for the first time.
  • Modal will run Vera alongside its existing Intel and AMD fleet in a mixed setup, assigning each job to whatever hardware performs best.
  • For Indian tech professionals and investors, the win is an early signal that the CPU layer of AI infrastructure — a roughly $200 billion market Nvidia is entering — is opening to a third competitor.

Nvidia has won central processor business with Modal, a fast-growing AI cloud startup that until now relied entirely on chips from Intel and AMD, according to Reuters. The deal is a design win, not an acquisition: Modal plans to start using Nvidia's new Vera central processor for hosting AI agents, the software systems that carry out long-running tasks for users, while keeping its existing suppliers in place.

Modal rents computing power to AI developers. Until this move, the CPU work behind its agent hosting ran only on Intel and AMD processors — the two companies that have long controlled the server CPU market Nvidia is now entering.

Tests that doubled agent output

Modal said on Monday that early tests showed the Vera chip doubled the amount of work AI agents can get done. That result prompted the company to support Nvidia's chip design for the first time, a step it acknowledged will require deep software changes on its side.

Chief Executive Erik Bernhardsson was careful to stress that Modal is not abandoning Intel or AMD. The company will run Nvidia chips alongside its current offerings in a mixed fleet, putting each job on whatever hardware runs it best. Bernhardsson noted the tests were run against Intel and AMD chips already on the market, and that both rivals have newer models in development that could narrow the gap.

"We'll test them when they're available. We can always deploy whatever hardware performs best."

— Erik Bernhardsson, CEO, Modal

A startup growing at unusual speed

Modal's endorsement carries weight because of its growth rate. The company last week raised $750 million in a funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation, and says it is on track to record $1 billion in sales over the next year. Usage of its services has tripled, and revenue has grown more than 15 times year over year, according to Reuters.

That growth is exactly the workload Vera was built for. As NVIDIA describes in its official Vera delivery account, AI agents do not run on GPUs alone: every agent sandbox, tool call, orchestration layer and long-context retrieval operation is CPU work. Vera packs 88 custom Olympus cores with 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth and, by Nvidia's own measurements, delivers up to 1.8 times faster per-core performance on agentic workloads.

Nvidia's $20 billion opening bid

Nvidia has told investors it expects to generate at least $20 billion from Vera chip sales this fiscal year — its opening bid for a CPU market it values at roughly $200 billion. Modal joins a customer list Nvidia has previously named that includes OpenAI, Anthropic and Oracle, along with AI startups such as Perplexity.

The significance for the wider industry is structural. For two decades, the economics of the data centre CPU were a two-vendor contest. Agentic AI changes what a CPU is for: instead of feeding a small number of GPUs, it must orchestrate thousands of concurrent, long-running agent tasks. If early adopters such as Modal find a twofold throughput gain holds in production, Intel and AMD face pressure not just on price but on architecture.

What to watch next

Two tests will decide whether this is a headline or a shift. First, whether Modal's production deployment confirms the doubling it saw in early tests once the required software work is done. Second, whether Intel's and AMD's next-generation server chips, which Bernhardsson says Modal will evaluate on arrival, close the performance gap. For now, Nvidia has its clearest evidence yet that its push beyond GPUs into the CPU socket has traction with the customers building the agent economy.
